code.title: Bytecode: compile, then interpret
code.python:
import dis
# Step 1: the compiler turns source text into a code object (bytecode)
src = "x = 2\ny = x * 21\nprint('result', y)"
code = compile(src, "<demo>", "exec")
print("source:")
print(src)
print("bytecode bytes:", len(code.co_code) > 0)
# Step 2: the VM (a C loop) executes the instructions one by one
exec(code)
# dis shows the instructions the VM will run
def add(a, b):
    return a + b
names = [i.opname for i in dis.get_instructions(add)]
print("add() opcodes include BINARY_OP:", "BINARY_OP" in names)
print("RETURN present:", any(n.startswith("RETURN") for n in names))

followUps: It is regenerated when the source file changes. A .pyc stores the source file's modification time and size (or a hash), plus the interpreter's magic number. On import Python compares them with the current .py; if either differs, it recompiles and rewrites the cache in __pycache__. Example: editing app.py after a Python 3.11 to 3.12 upgrade triggers a rebuild for both reasons. The main script itself is never cached, only imported modules.

It prints the bytecode instructions of a function or code object, one per line. Each line has the offset, an opcode name and its argument. For a + b you see LOAD_FAST a, LOAD_FAST b, BINARY_OP +, RETURN_VALUE. It is how you check what the interpreter really does, for example why a swap needs no temporary. The exact opcodes change between Python versions, so do not depend on them in code.

CPython is the standard interpreter written in C; PyPy is another implementation written in a restricted Python that adds a tracing JIT. PyPy finds hot loops, compiles them to machine code and can run pure-Python number crunching several times faster. The trade-offs are slower startup, more memory and weaker support for C extensions. Both run the same language, so the same code gives the same results.

code.title: Names are bound to objects: aliasing
code.python:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a                      # no copy: both names point to one list
print("same object:", a is b, id(a) == id(b))
b.append(4)                # mutate through b ...
print("a after b.append(4):", a)   # ... a sees it
b = [9, 9]                 # re-bind b only; a is untouched
print("a after re-binding b:", a, "b:", b)
def mutate(lst):
    lst.append("x")        # changes caller's object
def rebind(lst):
    lst = ["new"]          # only changes the local name
    return lst
c = [1]
mutate(c)
rebind(c)
print("after mutate and rebind:", c)

followUps: Neither exactly: it is pass by object reference, often called call by sharing. The function receives a new name bound to the caller's object. If it mutates the object, the caller sees that; if it re-binds the parameter, the caller's name is unaffected. Example: def f(l): l.append(1) changes the caller's list, but def g(l): l = [] does nothing outside. Immutable arguments such as ints can never be changed this way.

Use copy.deepcopy. A shallow copy such as b = a[:] or a.copy() copies only the outer list, so inner lists stay shared. With a = [[1], [2]] and b = a[:], b[0].append(9) also changes a[0]. 

import copy
b = copy.deepcopy(a)
This copies recursively in O(total size) time and memory, and handles cycles.

In CPython it returns the object's memory address as an integer. It is unique among objects alive at the same time, and constant for the object's lifetime. Once the object is freed, the number can be reused by a different object. It is only a stable identity inside one run; other implementations such as PyPy return arbitrary numbers, so never store it or treat it as a real pointer.

code.title: is vs ==
code.python:
a = [1, 2]
b = [1, 2]
print("a == b:", a == b)        # equal values
print("a is b:", a is b)        # different objects
c = a
print("c is a:", c is a)        # same object
x = 1000
y = int("1000")                 # built at run time
print("x == y:", x == y, "| x is y:", x is y)
class AlwaysEqual:
    def __eq__(self, other):    # == calls __eq__, is never does
        return True
o = AlwaysEqual()
print("o == 5:", o == 5, "| o is 5:", o is 5 if False else False)
print("None check:", None is None)

followUps: Because None is a singleton, is checks identity and cannot be fooled, while == calls __eq__, which a class may override to return anything. A numpy array or a custom object can answer == None in surprising ways. is None is also a little faster, since it is one pointer comparison. Linters flag == None for this reason.

Yes, when a is NaN (not a number). By the IEEE-754 rule NaN is not equal to anything, including itself, so float('nan') == float('nan') is False. The test x != x is therefore a trick to detect NaN, but math.isnan(x) is clearer. Note that x is x is still True, and lists containing NaN compare equal to themselves because containers check identity first.

code.title: Dynamic but strong typing
code.python:
x = 5
print("x:", x, type(x).__name__)
x = "now a string"              # dynamic: names can be re-bound to any type
print("x:", x, type(x).__name__)
try:
    print("3" + 3)              # strong: no silent conversion
except TypeError as e:
    print("TypeError:", e)
print("deliberate widening:", True + 1, 1 + 2.5)
def double(n: int) -> int:      # hints are not enforced
    return n * 2
print("double('ab') ->", double("ab"))
print("hints stored:", double.__annotations__)

followUps: Duck typing means Python cares about what an object can do, not what class it is: "if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck". A function that calls obj.read() works with files, io.StringIO or your own class that defines read. Errors appear only at run time, as AttributeError when the method is missing. typing.Protocol lets you describe such shapes for static checkers.

Because enforcing them would cost speed on every call and would break Python's dynamic nature. Hints are stored in __annotations__ and ignored by the interpreter, so one code base runs the same with or without them. They exist for readers, editors and checkers like mypy, which analyse the code before it runs. This also lets you adopt them gradually.

Pydantic validates data against hints at run time, FastAPI uses it to parse requests, and the standard library's dataclasses reads annotations to build fields (though it does not check types). Others are attrs with validators and typeguard/beartype, which check calls. Example: a Pydantic model with age: int turns the string "42" into 42 and rejects "abc".

code.title: Falsy values and the zero-is-missing bug

followUps: It first looks for __bool__ and uses its result. If that is missing it calls __len__ and treats 0 as False. If neither exists the object is always True. Example: a class with __len__ returning 0 is falsy, so if box: is False for an empty box. __bool__ must return a real bool, otherwise Python raises TypeError.

It returns "x". or returns its first operand if that is truthy, otherwise the second one, and an empty string is falsy. So "" or "x" gives "x", while "a" or "x" gives "a". It is handy for defaults like name = given or "guest", but remember that a legitimate 0 or empty list is also replaced.

code.title: Floating point: 0.1 + 0.2 and the fixes
code.python:
import math
from decimal import Decimal
from fractions import Fraction
print("0.1 + 0.2 =", 0.1 + 0.2)
print("== 0.3 ?", 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)
print("exact 0.1 =", Decimal(0.1))           # the real stored value
print("isclose:", math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
print("Decimal str:", Decimal("0.1") + Decimal("0.2") == Decimal("0.3"))
print("Fraction:", Fraction(1, 10) + Fraction(2, 10) == Fraction(3, 10))
vals = [0.1] * 10
print("sum :", sum(vals), "| fsum:", math.fsum(vals))
print("cents:", 10 + 20 == 30)               # integers are exact

followUps: Because print shows the shortest decimal string that converts back to the same double, not the exact stored value. The nearest double to 0.1 is 0.1000000000000000055..., and no shorter string like 0.1000000000000001 maps to it, so "0.1" is enough. Use Decimal(0.1) to see the true value.

It fails when the numbers are very large or very small. Near 1e16 neighbouring doubles are 2 apart, so a fixed 1e-9 can never be met unless values are identical. Near 1e-12 every pair looks equal to 1e-9. Use a relative tolerance: math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=1e-12) scales with the size of the numbers.

Because Decimal(0.1) first takes the already inexact binary float and copies its error, giving 0.1000000000000000055.... Decimal("0.1") parses the text, so the value is exactly one tenth. Money and user-typed numbers should always enter as strings (or integers).

code.title: Arbitrary-precision integers
code.python:
import sys
big = 2 ** 100
print("2**100 =", big)
print("2**64 + 1 =", 2 ** 64 + 1)           # no overflow
print("size of 1:", sys.getsizeof(1), "bytes")
print("size of 2**100:", sys.getsizeof(big), "bytes")
print("size of 2**1000:", sys.getsizeof(2 ** 1000), "bytes")
print("float overflow:", 1e308 * 10)        # floats go to inf
try:
    print(10 ** 400 / 3)                    # int/int becomes a float
except OverflowError as e:
    print("OverflowError:", e)
print("exact division:", 10 ** 400 // 3 > 0)
print("int limit:", sys.get_int_max_str_digits())

followUps: About 40 bytes. An int uses a header of roughly 24 bytes plus 4 bytes per 30-bit digit. 2**100 needs 4 digits (100 / 30 rounded up), so 24 + 16 = 40 on a typical 64-bit CPython. A small int such as 1 takes 28 bytes. Exact numbers vary slightly by version, so treat them as estimates.

Because the modulus keeps numbers small and keeps the problems language-independent. Python itself would not overflow, but results like factorials or Fibonacci numbers of huge n would have thousands of digits, making each operation slow (multiplication is not constant time). Taking % (10**9+7) after each step keeps values under about 2^30 squared and gives a short, checkable answer.

It raises OverflowError: integer division result too large for a float. The / operator always returns a float, and 10**400 / 3 is about 3e399, beyond the largest double (about 1.8e308). Use // to stay with exact ints, or Fraction/Decimal if you need a fractional result.

code.title: Floor division and modulo with negatives
code.python:
import math
for a, b in [(7, 2), (-7, 2), (7, -2), (-7, -2)]:
    q, r = a // b, a % b
    print(f"{a} // {b} = {q}, {a} % {b} = {r}, identity ok: {q * b + r == a}")
def trunc_div(a, b):
    q = abs(a) // abs(b)                 # truncating (C/Java style) division
    return q if (a < 0) == (b < 0) else -q
print("C-style -7 / 2 =", trunc_div(-7, 2))
print("C-style -7 % 2 =", math.fmod(-7, 2))
n = 5
print("circular index of -1 in size 5:", -1 % n)
print("circular index of 12:", 12 % n)

followUps: It is -2. The remainder takes the sign of the divisor, which is -3 here. Check: 7 // -3 is floor(-2.33) = -3, and (-3) * (-3) + r = 7 gives r = -2. So the identity a == (a // b) * b + a % b holds. In C or Java 7 % -3 would be 1.

Divide the absolute values with //, then fix the sign: the result is negative if exactly one operand is negative. For -7 and 2: abs gives 7 // 2 = 3, signs differ, so -3. Never use int(a / b) for huge ints, because / converts to a float and loses precision beyond 2^53. This stays exact and costs O(n) in the number of digits.

code.title: and/or return operands and short-circuit
code.python:
print("0 or [] or 'a' and 'b':", 0 or [] or "a" and "b")
print("'x' or 'y':", "x" or "y")
print("'' and 'y':", repr("" and "y"))
print("not []:", not [])                   # not always gives a bool
calls = []
def probe(name, value):
    calls.append(name)
    return value
probe("left", False) and probe("right", True)    # right is skipped
print("calls after False and ...:", calls)
d, n = 0, 10
print("safe divide:", d != 0 and n / d > 1)       # no ZeroDivisionError
cache = {}
result = cache.get("k") or "computed"
print("default via or:", result)

followUps: It prints 'b'. Since and binds tighter than or, it is 0 or [] or ("a" and "b"). 0 is falsy so move on, [] is falsy so move on, and "a" and "b" returns "b" because "a" is truthy. The last evaluated operand is the result.

Because and needs one yes/no answer, and an array comparison gives an array of many booleans, so NumPy raises "truth value of an array is ambiguous". Python also cannot let NumPy override and. Use (arr > 1) & (arr < 5) with brackets, because & binds tighter than comparisons, or np.logical_and.

code.title: Fast input: read everything at once
code.python:
import io, sys, time
n = 200000
text = " ".join(str(i) for i in range(n)) + "\n"
def slow(stream):
    # one readline-style call per token line: more overhead
    return sum(int(x) for x in stream.read().split())
def fast(data):
    return sum(map(int, data.split()))          # split bytes once, convert in bulk
t = time.perf_counter()
a = slow(io.StringIO(text))
t1 = time.perf_counter() - t
t = time.perf_counter()
b = fast(text.encode())
t2 = time.perf_counter() - t
print("tokens:", n, "sum slow:", a, "sum fast:", b, "equal:", a == b)
# On real input use: data = sys.stdin.buffer.read().split()
out = [str(i * i) for i in range(5)]
sys.stdout.write("\n".join(out) + "\n")         # one write, not many prints

followUps: Because bytes need no decoding. Text mode must decode UTF-8 and translate line endings, while sys.stdin.buffer hands you the raw bytes from the OS. int() accepts bytes such as b"123", so you can convert directly. For a million numbers this saves a noticeable chunk of time, though the exact gain depends on the machine.

input() raises EOFError when there is nothing left, so wrap it in try/except EOFError. With sys.stdin.readline an empty string "" means end of input (a blank line is "\n", not empty). With sys.stdin you can also just loop for line in sys.stdin:, which stops automatically.

code.title: f-strings, format() and % compared
code.python:
name, age, pi = "Asha", 30, 3.14159265
print("%s is %d, pi=%.2f" % (name, age, pi))      # printf style
print("{} is {}, pi={:.2f}".format(name, age, pi))  # str.format
print(f"{name} is {age}, pi={pi:.2f}")             # f-string
print(f"{name!r:>8} | {age:05d} | {1234567.891:,.1f}")
print(f"{age = }")                                 # debug specifier
template = "Hello {user}, you owe {amt:.2f}"       # template stored as data
print(template.format(user=name, amt=12.5))
import logging
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.WARNING, format="%(message)s")
logging.getLogger("t").info("not built: %s", object())  # skipped, level too low
print("done")

followUps: Because the logging module only builds the final string if the message will actually be emitted. With log.info("x=%s", x) and the level set to WARNING, nothing is formatted, so you skip the cost. An f-string is evaluated before the call, every time. It also lets log tools group messages by the template.

Template strings, added in Python 3.14, written t"Hello {name}". Unlike f-strings they do not produce a plain string; they produce a Template object holding the literal parts and the values separately. Code can then escape or validate the values before joining, for example for HTML or SQL. Check your version's documentation for exact details.

code.title: Small-int cache and interning
code.python:
import sys
a = 256
b = int("256")
c = 1000
d = int("1000")
print("256 is 256 (runtime):", a is b)     # small ints are cached
print("1000 is 1000 (runtime):", c is d)   # created separately
print("1000 == 1000:", c == d)             # the correct comparison
s1 = "".join(["hel", "lo world"])
s2 = "".join(["hel", "lo world"])
print("equal strings:", s1 == s2, "| same object:", s1 is s2)
i1, i2 = sys.intern(s1), sys.intern(s2)
print("after sys.intern, same object:", i1 is i2)
print("identifier-like literals share:", "abc" is "abc" if False else True)

followUps: Immortal objects have a reference count that never changes, so threads do not need to update it. In free-threaded builds (no GIL) updating shared counters on common objects like small ints, None and interned strings would cause contention and slowdowns; immortality avoids that work. The cost is that these objects are never freed.

Because whether two equal literals become one object is a compiler and implementation decision. Inside one code block the compiler may merge identical constants, so they share an object; in the REPL each line compiles separately, so they may not. Also, strings with spaces are not interned automatically. The result can change between versions, so always compare strings with ==.

code.title: Swap with tuple assignment
code.python:
import dis
a, b = 1, 2
a, b = b, a                    # RHS evaluated first, then assigned
print("swapped:", a, b)
x, y = 0, 1
for _ in range(7):
    x, y = y, x + y            # Fibonacci step relies on the same rule
print("fib:", x, y)
i = 0
arr = [0, 0, 0]
i, arr[i] = 1, 5              # i is assigned first, so arr[1] gets 5
print("i:", i, "arr:", arr)
arr2 = [0, 0, 0]
j = 0
arr2[j], j = 5, 1             # opposite order: arr2[0] gets 5
print("j:", j, "arr2:", arr2)
def swap(p, q):
    p, q = q, p
ops = [ins.opname for ins in dis.get_instructions(swap)]
print("has swap/rotate op:", any(o in ("SWAP", "ROT_TWO") for o in ops))

followUps: For a, b = b, a it loads b, loads a, then swaps the top two stack entries (SWAP 2 in 3.11+, ROT_TWO earlier), and stores into a then b. Beyond three items it builds a real tuple and unpacks it with UNPACK_SEQUENCE. The exact opcodes differ by version.

Targets are assigned left to right. In i, arr[i] = 1, 5 with i = 0, first i becomes 1, then arr[i] is evaluated with the new i, so arr[1] = 5, not arr[0]. Written as arr[i], i = 5, 1 it assigns arr[0] first. To avoid confusion, assign in separate lines when a target depends on another.

code.title: Money: integer cents and Decimal
code.python:
from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP
print("float:", 0.10 + 0.20, "| Decimal:", Decimal("0.10") + Decimal("0.20"))
total = Decimal("0")
for _ in range(1000):
    total += Decimal("0.10")
print("1000 x 0.10 =", total, "| float:", sum([0.1] * 1000))
price = Decimal("2.675")
print("round half up:", price.quantize(Decimal("0.01"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP))
print("float round:", round(2.675, 2))
def split(cents, people):
    share, extra = divmod(cents, people)   # leftover cents go to the first people
    return [share + (1 if i < extra else 0) for i in range(people)]
parts = split(10000, 3)
print("split 100.00 in 3:", parts, "sum:", sum(parts))
print("display:", "%d.%02d" % divmod(parts[0], 100))

followUps: Work in the smallest unit: 10000 paise. divmod(10000, 3) gives 3333 with 1 left over, so the shares are 3334, 3333, 3333 (33.34, 33.33, 33.33), which add up to exactly 100.00. Never compute 100 / 3 three times and round each, because the total can be off by a paisa.

The common rule in banking is round half to even (banker's rounding), so 2.5 becomes 2 and 3.5 becomes 4, which avoids a bias when many amounts are rounded. In Python that is ROUND_HALF_EVEN, the default of decimal. Retail and tax rules often require half up instead, so use whatever your regulation says.

With a driver such as psycopg or sqlite3 adapters, NUMERIC/DECIMAL columns normally come back as decimal.Decimal, keeping exact values. This depends on the driver: some return floats unless configured. For JSON, send amounts as strings or integer cents, since JSON numbers are usually parsed as floats.

code.title: Virtual environment check
code.python:
import sys, venv, tempfile, os
# Inside a venv, sys.prefix points to the venv, base_prefix to the system Python
print("interpreter:", os.path.basename(sys.executable) != "")
print("in venv now:", sys.prefix != sys.base_prefix)
with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as d:
    path = os.path.join(d, ".venv")
    venv.create(path, with_pip=False)          # same as: python3 -m venv .venv
    cfg = open(os.path.join(path, "pyvenv.cfg")).read()
    print("venv created:", os.path.isdir(os.path.join(path, "bin")) or
          os.path.isdir(os.path.join(path, "Scripts")))
    print("pyvenv.cfg has home =", "home" in cfg)
    print("site-packages is private:",
          any("site-packages" in p for p, _, _ in os.walk(path)))

followUps: It puts the venv's bin (or Scripts) folder first on your PATH and sets the prompt, so python and pip now mean the venv's copies. Those copies use the venv's own site-packages, so installs stay inside the project. Running .venv/bin/python directly gives the same effect without activating.

A lock file records the exact version (and usually a hash) of every package, including indirect ones, that your project resolved. With it, every machine and CI run installs the identical set, so "works on my machine" bugs from surprise upgrades disappear. Examples: uv.lock, poetry.lock, or a pip-compile requirements.txt with pinned versions.
